newsitem.title: GERMANY: German DyStar swings to profit, eyes rise in 97.
newsitem.headline: German DyStar swings to profit, eyes rise in 97.

text.p: Germany's DyStar Textilfarben GmbH, the world's leading textile dyestuff group, plans to double its profits this year as volume sales are expected to keep climbing and offset an ongoing drop in prices.
"Our goal is to double operating profits to 50 million marks ($29.5 million) in 1997," and raise turnover by 2.5 percent to 1.656 billion marks, general manager Alfred Rad told journalists.
Rad said business had got off to a strong start in the first four months of 1997 with sales in textile dyes jumping 14 percent.

In its first full year of operation DyStar, formed when German chemical giants Hoechst AG and Bayer AG merged their ailing textile dyes businesses, swung to an operating profit of 24 million marks with sales rising three percent to 1.616 billion marks.
Turnover was boosted by a seven-percent rise in volume sales, which was able to offset a five percent drop in prices.
"Our goal was to break even and we topped that," Rad said, explaining that the two separate groups' textile dyes units had jointly posted a loss of over 100 million marks in 1994.
DyStar benefited both from shifts in fashion taste towards more vibrant colours as well as a sharp reduction in costs.

The group's three main business units, reactive dyes, disperse dyes and special dyes, manufacture dyes used to colour a range of fabrics for clothing, carpets, upholstery and a variety of other products.

The strongest sales growth was seen in Asia, trailed by Turkey and eastern Europe, DyStar said, adding that sales in North America and western Europe reported only a small upturn as sluggish consumer demand helped dampen turnover.
By pooling Hoechst and Bayer's resources in improving capacity utilisation at its plants, DyStar managed to slice off 30 percent in costs.

As the restructuring programme continues, Rad said another 180 million marks or 15 percent in additional costs could be cut, moving the group closer to raising its return on sales from 1.8 percent at present to 10 percent in the next five years.
Based on last year's performance and expectations for this year, Rad said "we are now more sure that we can reach this goal."
To become more competitive in the lucrative Asian market, DyStar plans to expand its manufacturing and marketing capacities in Asia.
Joint ventures like ones formed in China and Indonesia are expected to increase in coming years even though Rad said there were no concrete plans for any new joint-ventures underway now.
This year DyStar hopes to raise its sales in Asia to 30 percent from 28 percent, Rad said.
While DyStar currently ranks as the world's largest textile dyestuffs company, German company BASF AG and Swiss groups Ciba and Clariant AG are following close behind.
DyStar was also put into a precarious situation when Hoechst late last year obtained a 45 percent stake in Clariant, thus holding a stake in two direct competitors.
While Rad said DyStar would be very interested in obtaining Clariant's textile dyestuff business, he said any decision about the matter would be made elsewhere.
"We are interested, but the decision making process rests with someone else," DyStar general manager Alfred Rad told a news conference.

A Hoechst spokesman said any competition issues arising between the two companies would have to be settled by these companies and that Hoechst had no plans to get involved in the situation. Clariant was not immediately available for comment.

Looking ahead, DyStar officials said privately that the company might consider seeking a separate bourse listing after completing all of its restructuring programmes. "That would be something to be considered," an official said, commenting on the trend for Hoechst units to spin off from the parent.
